title: Chapter XXXVIII — Conclusion
summary: Jane opens with the decisive statement that she married Rochester. Ten years later she describes a marriage of continuous conversation, mutual confidence, service without humiliation, and freedom within intimacy. Rochester recovers partial sight after two years and sees their firstborn son. Jane provides Adèle a kinder education; Diana and Mary make loving marriages and remain close. St. John never marries and spends his life in India, facing death with the same absolute faith and ambition that defined him.
events: Jane and Rochester marry quietly and establish their life at Ferndean.
Jane relocates Adèle to a kinder school and maintains a lasting relationship with her.
Rochester recovers limited sight and sees his firstborn son.
Diana and Mary marry happily; St. John remains an unmarried missionary and approaches death in India.

characters.name: Jane Eyre
characters.development: Narrates marriage as complete mutuality: her care is freely given and compatible with an undiminished self.

characters.name: Edward Rochester
characters.development: Accepts intimate dependence without shame and regains limited physical sight within a morally altered life.

characters.name: Adèle Varens
characters.development: Receives the humane education and continuing care that institutions earlier denied Jane.

characters.name: St. John Rivers
characters.development: Fulfills his chosen missionary vocation alone, with heroic constancy and an early death near.

threads.text: Jane achieves a home in which intimacy and freedom coexist.
Rochester's partial recovery and their child embody mercy after irreversible loss.
Jane's bonds with Adèle and the Rivers sisters continue beyond marriage.
St. John follows his missionary path without Rosamond or Jane and nears its end.
